stories.headline: Federal Judge Rules Pentagon Illegally Retaliated Against Anthropic Over AI Weapons Dispute
stories.summary:
A federal judge has ruled that the U.S. Department of Defense acted unlawfully when it designated AI startup Anthropic a supply-chain risk, calling the move "illegal and baseless." U.S. District Judge Rita Lin found that the Pentagon had orchestrated an unlawful boycott of the company after Anthropic refused to allow its AI models to be used for surveillance or autonomous weapons systems — the first time an American company had ever received such a designation.

Judge Lin wrote that invoking national security was "not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics," and said the government had sought to "cripple" the company and "chill public debate" over military use of AI. She described the Pentagon's actions as "classic First Amendment retaliation." The ruling follows a February designation under a law typically reserved for companies based in adversarial nations.

The dispute reflects a broader conflict between Silicon Valley AI firms and the Trump administration over the terms of military AI deployment. The White House had previously labeled Anthropic "a radical left, woke company attempting to control military activity," while the Pentagon argued that private firms should not be able to constrain military operations. Anthropic maintained its Claude models were not reliable enough for weapons systems and that domestic surveillance use would violate civil rights.

Anthropic welcomed the ruling, saying it remained focused on "working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit." The Pentagon and White House had not responded to requests for comment at time of publication. The case is expected to set a significant precedent for how the government can pressure private AI companies over military contracting terms.

stories.headline: Update: At Least 290 Indians Missing After Flash Floods Strike Nepal-Tibet Border During Kailash Pilgrimage
stories.summary:
At least 290 Indian citizens are reported missing after deadly flash floods struck along Nepal's border with Tibet, with many of the unaccounted for having been on a religious pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, a sacred site in Hinduism. The disaster unfolded on the morning of August 26, cutting off communication with large groups of pilgrims who had just crossed or were about to cross into Chinese-controlled Tibet.

Families in India described receiving final messages from loved ones moments before contact ceased entirely. Subhrasree Chakraborty, a 43-year-old medical technologist from Kolkata, sent her husband a photograph of her passport entry stamp at 7:57 a.m. local time and a message saying her group was waiting to enter China at 8:03 a.m. — then nothing. She was among roughly 30 people traveling together toward Kailash.

The Mount Kailash pilgrimage had only recently resumed after years of disruption from the COVID-19 pandemic and India-China border tensions. Thousands of Indians undertake the journey annually, traversing Nepal before entering Tibet. The flash floods struck a mountainous border zone where search and rescue operations are logistically difficult, compounding fears for survivors.

The scale of the missing persons count — 290 and rising — makes this one of the most significant disasters affecting Indian nationals abroad in recent years. Indian and Nepali authorities have launched search operations, but remote terrain and ongoing weather instability are hampering recovery efforts.

stories.headline: Dutch Court Sentences Man to Life in Prison for Role in 1994 Rwanda Genocide
stories.summary:
A court in The Hague has sentenced a 66-year-old Dutch-Rwandan man, identified only as Eugene N, to life in prison for his participation in the 1994 Rwandan genocide. The court convicted him of war crimes and genocide committed with "genocidal intent," finding that he had directed Hutu attackers at a football stadium where Tutsi civilians had sought shelter, instructing them not to let anyone escape. Survivors were killed with clubs and machetes.

Eugene N held an authoritative position as a local administrator in the Mbazi area of southern Rwanda during the genocide, overseeing approximately 1,000 people. The court found he had watched as homes were looted and burned before presiding over the stadium massacre. Rwanda had sought his extradition in 2014, but Dutch authorities opened their own investigation in 2020 after he had become a Dutch citizen; he was arrested in 2024.

The court stated that "only a lifelong prison sentence does justice to the immense suffering inflicted on the victims and bereaved families." Eugene N denied all charges, claiming he was himself a victim who had lost family members in the genocide. His defense lawyers said they would "almost certainly appeal" the conviction.

The case is among a series of prosecutions pursued in European courts under universal jurisdiction principles for crimes committed during the 100-day genocide, in which an estimated 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed by Hutu extremists in April 1994.

stories.headline: DHS Secretary Mullin Disputes Democrat's 'Kidnapping' Claim Over Deportation of 5-Year-Old With Father
stories.summary:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin pushed back Thursday against Texas Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico, who had publicly accused Immigration and Customs Enforcement of "kidnapping" a 5-year-old boy deported alongside his father. Victor Martinez Nieto and his son Liam Tadeo were removed from the United States on Tuesday after being detained in Austin, Texas, earlier this month while traveling to a soccer match.

Talarico, highlighting the case as part of his criticism of the Trump administration's immigration enforcement agenda, wrote on social media that Liam "should be in kindergarten" and had instead been thrown into "a prison camp hundreds of miles from home." The boy was reportedly set to begin kindergarten the week of his deportation. Talarico's framing drew significant attention on social media and in Democratic political circles.

Mullin responded by saying Talarico "won't tell the American people the full story," asserting that ICE does not separate families and that parents are asked whether they wish to be removed with their children or to designate a safe person for the child to remain with. "In this case, both the father and son were deported together," Mullin wrote. DHS also noted that Martinez Nieto had previously been arrested in November 2025, deported in February 2026, and had re-entered the country illegally before his second detention.

The dispute illustrates the sharp political divide over immigration enforcement, with Democrats arguing the administration is separating children from their futures and communities, while Republicans contend that enforcement is being applied lawfully and that parents bear responsibility for the consequences of illegal re-entry. The case has become a focal point in the competitive Texas Senate race.

stories.headline: King Harald V of Norway Dies at 89; Son to Reign as Haakon VIII
stories.summary:
King Harald V of Norway, Europe's oldest reigning monarch, died peacefully Friday morning at the national hospital in Oslo at age 89. The royal palace announced he passed away at 06:35 local time after being hospitalized for a rare blood condition. His son will ascend to the throne as King Haakon VIII.

Harald V had reigned for 35 years and was known internationally as a three-time Olympic yachtsman. He was widely regarded as a monarch who broke with royal tradition, including by marrying a commoner — Sonja Haraldsen — over objections from the Norwegian government, a decision that required a years-long public campaign before parliament ultimately consented.

His death marks a historic transition for Norway's constitutional monarchy. Harald's passing closes a reign that spanned major shifts in Norwegian society and politics, from the country's transformation into one of the world's wealthiest nations through North Sea oil revenues to its prominent role in international diplomacy and peace negotiations.

The succession follows established Norwegian constitutional procedure, with Crown Prince Haakon, 52, immediately assuming the throne. Norway has not yet announced details of state funeral arrangements.

stories.headline: Congo Launches Ebola Vaccinations as Outbreak Becomes Deadliest in Country's History
stories.summary:
The Democratic Republic of Congo on Thursday officially launched an Ebola vaccination campaign in Kisangani, capital of Tshopo province, as the country battles its worst Ebola outbreak on record. Health Minister Roger Kamba announced the campaign, with frontline health workers and close contacts of confirmed patients among the first to receive doses of the Ervebo vaccine.

As of Tuesday, Congo had recorded 5,713 confirmed cases and 2,744 deaths — a fatality rate of approximately 48 percent across six affected provinces including Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Tshopo, Haut-Uele and Bas-Uele. The World Health Organization has warned the outbreak remains out of control and is on track to surpass the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic, which killed more than 11,000 people and stands as the deadliest Ebola outbreak in history.

A significant scientific complication shadows the campaign: the current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola virus, while Ervebo is approved specifically against the Zaire strain. The vaccine is being administered under a compassionate-use program, with data to be collected simultaneously in a clinical trial to measure its actual effectiveness against Bundibugyo Ebola, for which no approved vaccine currently exists.

The outbreak is spreading under extremely difficult conditions, compounded by ongoing armed insecurity, mass population displacement, a health workers' strike, and intense cross-border movement in eastern Congo. More than 50,000 doses have been received, with the campaign targeting 14 health zones across three provinces.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. Military Clears All Iranian Sea Mines from Strait of Hormuz Transit Routes
stories.summary:
U.S. Central Command announced Thursday that American forces have cleared all Iranian sea mines along internationally recognized shipping lanes in the Strait of Hormuz, describing it as a major milestone in the ongoing standoff with Iran. CENTCOM Commander Admiral Brad Cooper made the announcement in a video posted to social media, marking a concrete new operational development in what has been a prolonged crisis affecting global oil markets.

The clearance of the mines represents a significant shift in the physical status of the waterway, through which roughly 20 percent of global oil supplies transit. Prior coverage had focused on diplomatic efforts, sanctions pressure, and the broader strategic standoff; Thursday's announcement is the first confirmation that the mines themselves have been neutralized along recognized transit corridors.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has separately argued that oil pipeline infrastructure will render the Strait of Hormuz strategically irrelevant within two years, a claim energy experts have disputed as unrealistic given current infrastructure timelines and capacity constraints. Iran, meanwhile, has been touting a separate plan involving Oman to restore shipping movement through the strait, signaling the diplomatic dimension remains unresolved even as the immediate navigational hazard has been addressed.

The development is likely to affect oil prices and shipping insurance rates in the near term, though the broader U.S.-Iran standoff, including sanctions and the status of any diplomatic framework, remains unsettled.

stories.headline: Stars and Stripes Publisher, Editor-in-Chief Sue Pentagon Over Firings, Citing First Amendment
stories.summary:
The publisher, editor-in-chief, and a reporter for Stars and Stripes — a congressionally chartered, government-funded news outlet serving U.S. military personnel — filed a federal lawsuit Thursday against the Department of Defense, seeking to reverse last week's firings. Publisher Max Lederer, Editor-in-Chief Erik Slavin, and reporter Lara Korte filed the complaint in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, alleging the terminations were unlawful and violated First Amendment protections.

The lawsuit alleges the Pentagon retaliated against the journalists for reporting on the USS Abraham Lincoln, according to court filings. Stars and Stripes, which the complaint describes as the U.S. military's independent news service, has operated for decades with an editorial firewall intended to insulate its journalism from command influence. The plaintiffs argue the firings breach both that statutory independence and constitutional free-speech protections.

The Department of Defense has not publicly detailed its rationale for the terminations. The case raises broader questions about press freedom within government-funded media and the limits of executive authority over outlets that receive federal funding but are structured to maintain editorial independence.

The lawsuit is being closely watched by press-freedom advocates and military journalists. Democrats and some Republicans have previously pushed back against administration moves affecting Stars and Stripes, which has served troops in war zones since the Civil War era. No court date has been set.
